transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

They sent me in from work. I guess I was… arranging some of the airway bags in the bay, putting them in the pattern that felt right. I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud, too.

My lieutenant told me to stop, but I couldn’t really step away. It felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would… go bad. So they brought me here.
When you were arranging the bags, did it feel like you had to do it to prevent something bad from happening?

Yeah… sort of. It wasn’t like I had a clear picture of something happening. It just felt like if I stopped or got the order wrong, the whole bay would go bad. So I kept moving the airway bags and saying the dispatch numbers. I couldn’t really step away when he told me to.
When you were saying the dispatch numbers out loud, did it feel like something that just burst out on its own?

Not exactly burst out… I mean, I was saying them because they had to be said with the pattern. The airway bags had to be in the right order, and if I stopped, it felt like the bay would go bad. I just… couldn’t step away when he told me to.
While this was happening, did you believe the bay would literally be harmed if you stopped?

Not the bay exactly… it’s more that people are watching what I do there. The injury review people, some supervisors. Through the cameras. And then things in my triage notes get changed so it looks like I’m unsafe.

They say it’s routine paperwork, but… I know what it is.
Do you think it’s possible you could be mistaken about the cameras and your notes being changed?
I don’t think so. I know what they tell me, that it’s just routine paperwork or whatever, but… the cameras are there, and the notes get changed. It’s not just me misunderstanding it.
Have you ever heard voices speaking to you when no one was there?
I… I don’t know. Not like someone standing in the room talking to me. I haven’t really noticed that.
When you were arranging the bags and saying the numbers, did any part of you feel that it didn’t really make sense?

Some part of me knew it probably looked strange, yeah. But at the time it felt… right. Like the airway bags had to be in that pattern, and the dispatch numbers had to be said the right way. If I stopped or stepped away, it felt like the bay would go bad somehow.
How long have you been having these concerns about being watched through the cameras and your notes being changed?
I guess… around two months. That’s when the camera stuff and the notes changing really started getting hard to ignore.
When the urge to arrange the bags and say the numbers comes up, does it feel like an unwanted thought or urge coming from your own mind?

I don’t know if I’d call it unwanted. It felt like… something I had to do. The bags had to be in that pattern, and the dispatch numbers had to be said right. If I stopped, it felt like the whole bay would go bad.
During these past two months, have you had a period where you felt unusually high, energized, or euphoric for days at a time?
Not really. I mean… I’ve been on edge, but not high or euphoric for days or anything like that.
Do these urges to arrange the bags and say the numbers feel intrusive and unwanted to you?

Not exactly unwanted. I mean… I didn’t want trouble, but it felt like I had to keep doing it. The bags had to be in the right pattern, and the numbers had to be said right. If I stopped or walked away, it felt like the bay would go bad somehow.
When you’re doing the arranging and saying the numbers, does any part of you feel that it doesn’t actually make sense?

I mean… part of me knows it probably looks strange. But when I was doing it, it felt like the bags had to be in that pattern, and the numbers had to come out right. I couldn’t just step away when he told me to. It felt like if I broke it, the bay would go bad.
At the time you were arranging the bags and saying the numbers, were you certain that doing it was truly necessary?

Yeah… at the time, I was pretty sure. It felt necessary. Like if I didn’t keep the bags in the right pattern and say the dispatch numbers right, something in the bay was going to go wrong. I couldn’t just stop when he told me to.
Do you believe that arranging the bags and saying the numbers really prevents something bad from happening?

I… yeah, I guess I did believe that. At least right then. If I didn’t keep the bags in the right order and say the numbers right, it felt like the whole bay would go bad somehow. I know that sounds… but I couldn’t just break the sequence.
Have you heard voices when no one else was around?
I don’t know… I haven’t really noticed that. Not like someone standing there talking when nobody’s around.
During these past two months, have you had a period of feeling very depressed for days at a time?
I’m not sure… I mean, I’ve felt worn down, but I don’t know if I’d call it depressed for days. I haven’t really been keeping track.
During these past two months, have you had a time when you felt depressed nearly all day, almost every day?
I don’t know. I’ve been… off, I guess, but I can’t say it was nearly all day every day. I haven’t really thought about it like that.
During these past two months, have the camera concerns and note-changing beliefs been there even when your mood felt basically normal?

Yeah… it’s not really tied to my mood. Even when I feel basically normal, I still know the cameras at the station are being used to watch me, and that some of the supervisors or injury review people have been changing my triage notes to make me look unsafe. They say it’s just routine paperwork, but… I don’t buy that.
Have you heard a voice talking about you when no one else was there?
Not that I’ve noticed. I mean… I don’t think so. If no one’s there, I’m usually just hearing my own thoughts, I guess.
Have people told you lately that your speech was hard to follow or didn’t make sense?
Not really. I mean, maybe people ask me to repeat myself sometimes, but nobody’s said I’m not making sense.

final_diagnosis.reason: The presentation is most consistent with an acute psychotic disorder: fixed persecutory beliefs about cameras and supervisors altering notes for about two months, poor insight, and behavior driven by a delusional sense of necessity. Schizoaffective disorder is less likely because no clear manic or major depressive episode was established, and the psychotic symptoms occur outside mood changes.
